lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Together, we can make the world a better place. Today, the beam of light from the Round Table turns into a stairway of light. Each step glows softly and rings like a tiny bell when we step on it. We climb up and up, through the clouds, holding hands. Birimo hums a happy song the whole way. At the top, we find a quiet garden of light. The grass is soft and silver, little lights float in the air like fireflies, and in the middle there is a calm pool of starlight. Then a tiny glowing star-creature flies toward us. Her voice sounds like a soft bell. She says, Welcome, friends. I'm Celeste, the keeper of this star. Shine on! She tells us that this is the Star of Beginnings. Haru remembers Orbit's words and says them again. This star shows where every journey began. Say it with me. This star shows where every journey began. Wonderful! Celeste points to a silver sign in the grass. Let's read Celeste's welcome words. "Welcome to the Star of Beginnings. Every journey with words begins with a small light. Maybe it is the first time you say hello, or the first word you can read. This star keeps all of those little lights, and today it keeps yours, too. Look up. The star has six points, or rays. Right now, all six rays are dim. As you look back on your adventures and get ready for what comes next, something wonderful will happen. Take your time here, my little lights. Rest on the soft silver grass, look into the pool, and remember how far you have come. Shine on!" What does every journey with words begin with? A small light. How many rays does the star have? Six, and right now they are all dim. Celeste flies around Birimo once and gives him a little smile, as if she already knows him. Birimo blinks and asks, Have we met before? Celeste only giggles. Now, phonics. Let's look back at some spelling patterns from our first years. Rain has a and i in the middle. Play has a and y at the end. Dream has e and a in the middle. They all make long sounds, and each spelling has its own place. Next time, the pool of starlight will show us a very special memory.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This star shows where every journey began. Today, Celeste leads us to the calm pool of starlight. Look into the pool, she says softly. It remembers everything. At first, we only see our own faces. Then the water ripples, and a picture appears. It's a green forest with tall trees and a little path. It's the Forest of Beginnings! We see a small boy and a small girl standing under a tree. They look so young! Haru laughs and points at the pool. That's me! And that's you, Riko! Then Haru turns to all of us. Do you remember our first lesson? We said, Hello! I'm Haru. Say it with me. Do you remember our first lesson? We said, Hello! I'm Haru. Wonderful! A memory page floats up from the water, shining like the moon. Let's read the memory page. "Memory Page: The Forest of Beginnings. On the very first day, the forest was green and quiet. A boy waved and said, Hello! I'm Haru. A girl smiled and said, Hi! I'm Riko. Nice to meet you. Then Ms. Emma taught four magic words with actions: Look! Stop! Come here! Go! Everybody pointed, froze, waved and ran. On the second day, a girl named Kiko waved and said, Bye, Haru! A few days later, a round, fluffy friend yawned and said, I'm sleepy. But when the children played with him, he jumped up and shouted, Yes! I'm happy now! That fluffy friend was Birimo." What were the four magic words? Look! Stop! Come here! Go! How did Birimo feel at first? He was sleepy. Everyone looks at Birimo, and we all laugh. Birimo covers his face with his paws. I was very young then! Celeste smiles at him again, and her light twinkles. I smile warmly and say, You have all grown so much. Now, phonics. Let's review three more spelling patterns. Green has two e's in the middle. Boat has o and a in the middle. Snow has o and w at the end. Boat and snow have the same sound, but o, a goes in the middle and o, w goes at the end. Next time, we'll talk about everything we can do now.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Do you remember our first lesson? We said, Hello! I'm Haru. Today, we sit on the silver grass next to the pool of starlight. Celeste floats down and asks a gentle question. Little lights, what can you do now that you couldn't do before? We all start talking at once! Riko can write her own stories. Haru can explain how deep-sea fish make light. Kiko can talk about feelings and listen kindly. Birimo can order pancakes in five different ways. I laugh and give everyone a piece of glowing paper. Let's make a can-do list! Kiko looks at all the papers and says, I've learned so much since I started. Say it with me. I've learned so much since I started. Super! Kiko reads her can-do list first. Let's read Kiko's can-do list. "My Can-Do List. Six years ago, I could only say hello and bye-bye. I've learned so much since I started! Now I can read whole books in English, and I can tell my own stories. I can give a short presentation and answer questions about it. I can share my opinion and listen to a different opinion kindly. I can talk about my feelings and help a friend who feels sad. I can read a map, ask for directions and order food. I've made friends from many places, and I've met amazing guides like Ember, Skye and Orbit. I still make mistakes, but now I know that mistakes help me learn." What could Kiko say six years ago? Only hello and bye-bye. What does Kiko know about mistakes now? Mistakes help her learn. Celeste's light grows a little warmer as she listens. Shine on! she whispers. Haru adds one more line to his list: I can be patient when something is hard. Now, phonics. Light has i, g and h, and the g and h are silent. Shirt has i and r, and i, r sounds just like u, r and e, r. Phone starts with p and h, but p, h sounds like f. Next time, we'll talk about our favorite worlds.

lines.speaker: Haru

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I've learned so much since I started. Today, the pool of starlight shows a different world each time Celeste touches the water. We see the Harbor of the World, the Rainbow Bridge, the City of Tomorrow and the Hall of Wisdom. Each picture makes us shout, I remember that! Celeste asks, Which world did you like best? Riko answers first, because she already knows. My favorite world was the Labyrinth of Tales because I loved writing stories. Say it with me. My favorite world was the Labyrinth of Tales because I loved writing stories. Great job! Riko writes a favorite-world card and reads it to us. Let's read Riko's card. "My Favorite World by Riko. My favorite world was the Labyrinth of Tales because I loved writing stories. Every path in the maze told a different story. Nib, the little mouse, helped us find six golden pages. I learned how to start a story, how to show feelings without saying them, and how to end a story with a surprise. The highlight was the storytelling night. I was nervous, but I paused at the most exciting part and lowered my voice. Everyone leaned in, and at the end, they clapped and cheered. Since that night, I've written a new story almost every week. Stories make me feel brave, and they help me understand other people." Who helped the friends find the golden pages? Nib, the little mouse. What was the highlight for Riko? The storytelling night. Then the others share. Haru loved Deep Sea City, because the glowing fish looked like stars under the sea. Kiko loved the Highlands of the Heart, because she learned to listen to her friends' feelings. And Birimo? He loved the Bustling Market. Food! he shouts. Now, phonics. Some letters are silent. Knee starts with k and n, but we don't say the k. Wrong starts with w and r, but we don't say the w. Thumb ends with m and b, but we don't say the b. Next time, we'll make a timeline of our whole journey.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, My favorite world was the Labyrinth of Tales because I loved writing stories. Today, we make a long timeline on the silver grass. I give everyone six glowing ribbons, one for each year of our journey. We write the most important memories on each ribbon and lay them in a line. Then we stand at the start of the timeline, and Celeste floats in front of us, ready to listen. Haru and Riko present the first part together. In the first year, we learned to say hello. By the third year, we could tell stories. Say it with me. In the first year, we learned to say hello. By the third year, we could tell stories. Excellent! Then each of us reads one part of the timeline. Let's read our timeline. "Our Journey Timeline. Year One: In the Forest of Beginnings, we learned to say hello, count and name colors. Year Two: In the Kingdom of English, Birimo found a glowing map of worlds that were not on any map yet. Year Three: In the Ruins of Memory, we read our first real stories. Year Four: We made video calls, read books in the Amber Library and acted in plays. Year Five: We shared opinions at the Lighthouse of Ideas and designed inventions in the City of Tomorrow. Year Six: We gave presentations, wrote our own stories, learned about feelings and joined a children's conference. Every year, we grew a little more, together." What did Birimo find in Year Two? A glowing map. Where did the friends read their first real stories? In the Ruins of Memory. When we finish, the star begins to hum softly. One of the six rays starts to glow, brighter and brighter. Riko shouts, The Ray of Memories lit up! Celeste claps her tiny hands and says, You remembered every step. Shine on! Birimo counts on his paws and says, One down, five to go! Now, phonics. Let's review. Rain has a, i in the middle. Snow has o, w at the end. Phone has p, h, which sounds like f. Thumb has a silent b at the end. Next time, we'll open our portfolios and choose our best work.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, In the first year, we learned to say hello. By the third year, we could tell stories. Today, Celeste gives each of us a shining folder. Inside is our portfolio（作品集）, a collection of our best work from six years. There are stories, speeches, letters, posters and even recordings of our voices. Riko opens her folder and gasps. My first story is in here! It's only three lines long! We all flip through our folders and laugh at our early drawings. Then I ask everyone to choose one piece of work that makes them really proud. Riko chooses right away. She holds up a thick stack of pages with a golden cover. This is the story I wrote in World 37. Say it with me. This is the story I wrote in World 37. Wonderful! Riko reads the label she wrote for it. Let's read Riko's portfolio label. "My Best Work: The Moon Fox. This is the story I wrote in World 37, in the Labyrinth of Tales. It's about a little fox who wants to touch the moon. At first, the fox is unhappy because the moon is too far away. Then she learns that the moon's light touches her softly every night. I chose this story because I worked on it for a long time. I had to rewrite the ending three times! Nib the mouse gave me great ideas, and my friends helped me make the middle more exciting. When I read it on storytelling night, everyone clapped. It shows that I can write a whole story in English." How many times did Riko rewrite the ending? Three times. Why did she choose this story? Because she worked on it for a long time. Haru chooses his deep-sea presentation from World 36. Kiko chooses her opening speech from the Round Table. And Birimo proudly holds up a pancake recipe card from the market. It's a classic! he says. Now, phonics. Unhappy is un plus happy, so it means not happy. Rewrite is re plus write, so it means write again. Preview is pre plus view, so it means look before. Next time, we'll compare the old us and the new us.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, This is the story I wrote in World 37. Today, I draw a big chart on a sheet of light. On the left side, it says Me Then. On the right side, it says Me Now. Celeste explains that the pool of starlight can show both. When Kiko looks into the water, she sees a tiny Kiko hiding behind a tree in the Forest of Beginnings. Then the water ripples, and she sees herself at the Round Table, giving the opening speech in front of children from all over the world. Kiko smiles and says, At first, I could only say hello. Now, I can give a speech in English. Say it with me. At first, I could only say hello. Now, I can give a speech in English. Fantastic! Kiko fills in her chart and reads it to us. Let's read Kiko's chart. "Me Then, Me Now by Kiko. Me then: I was very shy. I used to hide when someone talked to me. I could only say hello and bye-bye, and I didn't like reading aloud. Me now: I enjoy meeting new friends, and I can ask them questions. I can read long stories aloud with feeling. At first, I could only say hello. Now, I can give a speech in English! I used to be careless with spelling, but now I check my writing carefully. I still feel nervous sometimes, but I have learned to take a deep breath and smile. The biggest change is this: I believe in myself now." What did Kiko use to do when someone talked to her? She used to hide. What is Kiko's biggest change? She believes in herself now. Haru's chart says he used to think English was too hard, but now he reads science books for fun. Riko used to write only three lines, but now she writes whole stories. Birimo used to fall asleep in lessons. And now? He only falls asleep after lunch. Now, phonics. Dislike is dis plus like, so it means the opposite of like. Careful is care plus f, u, l, so it means full of care. Careless is care plus less, so it means without care. Careful and careless are opposites. Next time, we'll talk about the hardest parts of our journey.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, At first, I could only say hello. Now, I can give a speech in English. Today, Celeste asks a brave question. Little lights, what was the hardest part of your journey? Everyone is quiet for a moment. Then Haru laughs. Past tense! I used to say goed and eated. Riko says R and L were hard for her, because right and light sounded the same at first. Birimo says the hardest part was waiting for his turn. Everyone giggles. Then Kiko takes a deep breath. The hardest part was speaking in front of people, but I kept going. Say it with me. The hardest part was speaking in front of people, but I kept going. Great job! Kiko shows us a page from her diary. Let's read Kiko's hard-parts diary. "My Hard-Parts Diary. In the third year, I had to read a short poem in front of the class. My hands were shaking, and my voice was very small. I read too quickly, and I made two mistakes. That night, I felt sad. But Ms. Emma said, Being nervous means you care. My friends practiced with me every day. Riko clapped, Haru gave me a thumbs-up, and Birimo made funny faces so I would relax. Little by little, my voice got stronger. The hardest part was speaking in front of people, but I kept going. Last month, I gave the opening speech at the Round Table. My friends' kindness helped me so much." Why did Kiko feel sad that night? Because she read too quickly and made two mistakes. What did Birimo do to help? He made funny faces so she would relax. Celeste shines warmly and says, Hard parts are part of every journey. Shine on! I add, Every one of you kept going, and that is what matters most. Now, phonics. Kindness is kind plus ness, and ness makes a noun. Quickly is quick plus l, y, and l, y tells us how. Movement is move plus ment, and ment makes a noun, too. Next time, we'll make cards for children who are just starting to learn English.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The hardest part was speaking in front of people, but I kept going. Today, the pool of starlight shows something new. We see the Forest of Beginnings again, but this time, we are not in the picture. Instead, we see a group of new first-year children standing under the trees with their teacher. One little boy waves and says, Hello! Everyone gasps. They're just starting, like we did! Celeste asks us to write advice cards for them. Riko thinks for a moment and writes the first card. My advice is to listen to English every day. Say it with me. My advice is to listen to English every day. Perfect! Then we all write our cards together. Let's read our advice cards. "Advice Cards for New Learners. From Riko: My advice is to listen to English every day. Songs, stories and cartoons all help. From Haru: Don't be afraid of mistakes. I made so many mistakes, and they taught me a lot. From Kiko: Read aloud, even if you feel shy. Your voice will get stronger, little by little. From Birimo: Sing songs! Singing makes English feel comfortable, like a warm pancake. From all of us: Learning a new language may seem impossible at first, but it isn't. Take one small step every day. Be kind to yourself, and ask your friends and teachers for help. You can do it! We believe in you." What does Birimo say singing does? It makes English feel comfortable. What does Haru say about mistakes? Don't be afraid of them, because they teach you a lot. Celeste gathers the cards. Each card turns into a tiny light, and the lights float down, down, down to the forest. The new children look up and smile. Now, phonics. Invention is invent plus i, o, n, and i, o, n makes a noun. Comfortable is comfort plus able, so it means nice and cozy. Impossible is im plus possible, so it means not possible. Before p, we use im, not in. Next time, we'll show our portfolios to Celeste and me.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, My advice is to listen to English every day. Today is our portfolio showcase. Celeste and I sit on the silver grass, and the floating lights gather around us to listen. Each of us has five minutes to present our best work. Haru goes first. He stands up straight, takes a deep breath, smiles, opens his folder and says, Let me show you my portfolio. Say it with me. Let me show you my portfolio. Excellent! Haru begins with the very first page. Let's read Haru's portfolio introduction. "Let me show you my portfolio. On the first page, there is a drawing of a fish from Year One. Under it, I wrote one word: fish. On the next pages, you can see how my writing grew. In Year Three, I wrote short diaries. In Year Five, I made a poster about an invention that cleans the sea. My best work is my deep-sea presentation from World 36. It explains how some deep-sea fish make their own light. I was unhappy with my first draft because it was too long, so I made it shorter and clearer. I practiced my hand movements and spoke slowly. This shows that I can explain science in English. My dream is to keep learning about the ocean. Do you have any questions?" What did Haru write under his first drawing? One word: fish. Why was Haru unhappy with his first draft? Because it was too long. Then Riko, Kiko and Birimo present, too. Celeste asks careful questions, and everyone answers clearly. Birimo even explains how his recipe card shows his growth: his first pancake was flat, but his last one was fluffy! When the last folder closes, the star hums, and the second ray begins to glow. Kiko shouts, The Ray of Growth lit up! Celeste rings like a bell and says, You have grown so much. Shine on! Now, phonics. Let's review. Unhappy is un plus happy. Careful is care plus f, u, l. Movement is move plus ment. Dream has e, a in the middle. Next time, we'll start practicing for an interview test, and the first question will be all about you.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let me show you my portfolio. Two rays of the star are shining now. Today, Celeste has a new idea. She says, Many learners take a speaking test at the end of a long trip with words. It isn't scary. It's a chance to show how much you've grown. Celeste makes a little room of light with a table and two chairs. I sit behind the table. I will be the examiner. Birimo jumps into the other chair and says, I'm playing the examiner, too! You can have a turn later, Birimo. First, we practice how an interview begins. You knock on the door, walk in, and say good morning. Then you wait until the examiner says, Please sit down. The first question is often the same. Please tell me about yourself. Say it with me. Please tell me about yourself. Wonderful! In our practice, you answer as your story self. You don't need to say your real name or your school. A nickname is fine. Let's read the interview guide. "Interview Guide. Step one: Knock on the door, walk in, and say good morning or hello. Step two: Sit down when the examiner asks you to. Sit up straight and smile. Step three: Listen carefully. When the examiner says, Please tell me about yourself, talk about the things you like. You can talk about your hobbies, your favorite food, or something fun you do on weekends. Try to say three or four sentences, and add a reason or an example. Step four: When the examiner says thank you, say thank you, too, and walk out calmly. Don't worry about small mistakes. Examiners want to hear your ideas, not perfect English." What should you do when you sit down? Sit up straight and smile. How many sentences should you try to say? Three or four. Haru goes first. He says, I love swimming. I go to the pool every weekend, and I also like reading about sea animals. I nod. That was clear and friendly. Celeste looks at Birimo with a little smile, as if she knows something about him. Now, phonics. Some long words share a root. Inspect has spect, which means look, like spectator. Construct has struct, which means build, like structure. Predict has dict, which means say, like dictionary. Next time, we'll talk about a picture in an interview.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Please tell me about yourself. All four of us practiced our self-introductions, and even Birimo answered without talking about pancakes for a whole minute. Today, I bring out a picture card. In many interview tests, the examiner shows you a picture and asks you about it. You don't need to tell a story. You just say what you can see, clearly and calmly. I hold up the card. It shows a sunny park. I point to the boy and ask the question. Look at the picture. What is the boy doing? Say it with me. Look at the picture. What is the boy doing? Great! The answer uses the ing form, because it's happening in the picture right now. He's walking a dog. Let's read the model answer for the picture card. "In this picture, I can see a sunny park. There are tall trees and a small pond. A boy is walking a dog. The dog has a red leash, and it looks very happy. Under a big tree, a girl is reading a book. Maybe it's an exciting story, because she's smiling. In the middle of the park, two children are flying a kite. The kite is shaped like a fish, and it's very high in the sky. Near the gate, a man is selling ice cream from a little cart. There are three people waiting in line. I think it's a hot day, because everyone wants ice cream." What is the girl doing? She's reading a book under a tree. How many people are waiting for ice cream? Three. I explain a useful trick. First, say the big picture, like There are tall trees. Then talk about each person with is and ing. Finally, add one small idea of your own, like I think it's a hot day. Then Birimo grabs the picture card and says, I'm playing the examiner! He asks Haru about the boy, Kiko about the kite, and then he stops and stares at the ice cream cart for a very long time. Celeste giggles like a little bell. Now, phonics. Erupt has rupt, which means break, like interrupt. Project has ject, which means throw, like reject. Transport has port, which means carry, like export. Next time, we'll give our opinions and our reasons.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Look at the picture. What is the boy doing? We described the park, and Birimo finally got his ice cream, at least in his imagination. Today, we practice the hardest part of the interview: giving an opinion. I show everyone an opinion card with one question on it. Do you think more people will ride bikes in the future? Why? Say it with me. Do you think more people will ride bikes in the future? Why? Great job! Kiko looks worried and asks, What if I give the wrong answer? I smile. In an opinion question, there is no wrong answer. You can say I think so, or I don't think so. The examiner wants to hear what you think and why. Try to give two reasons. Let's read the opinion card. "Opinion Card. Question: Do you think more people will ride bikes in the future? Why? Answer A: I think so, for two reasons. First, riding a bike is good for your health. Second, bikes don't make the air dirty, so more people will choose them to keep the air fresh. Answer B: I don't think so, for two reasons. First, some towns have a lot of steep hills, and riding up them is very tiring. Second, it's hard to carry heavy groceries on a bike, especially for a big family. Both answers are good answers. Each one gives a clear opinion, two reasons, and the words first and second." What are the two reasons in Answer A? Riding a bike is good for your health, and bikes don't make the air dirty. Does the examiner want one special answer? No. Any opinion is fine if you give reasons. Then we try it. Riko says she thinks so, because new bike lanes are safe and there are fewer traffic jams. Haru says he doesn't think so, because rain makes riding hard. Kiko nods and says, That's a good point. I didn't think about rainy days. Celeste rings softly and says, Two friends, two opinions, and both of them are kind. Now, phonics. Visible has vis, which means see, like vision. Describe has scrib, which means write, like scribble. Audience has aud, which means hear, like audio. Next time, we'll practice what to say when we don't hear a question.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Do you think more people will ride bikes in the future? Why? Riko and Haru had different opinions, and both of them gave two good reasons. Today, Birimo wants to be the examiner again. I agree, but there is one problem. Birimo is eating a pancake! He asks Kiko a question, but his mouth is full, and he mumbles. Mmf mmf favorite mmf? Kiko doesn't understand. In a real interview, the examiner won't eat pancakes, but sometimes you won't hear the question. The room might be noisy, or the examiner might speak quickly. That's OK. You can ask politely. Could you say that again, please? Say it with me. Could you say that again, please? Perfect! Asking again isn't a mistake. It shows that you really want to understand. Let's read the tips for interviews. "Tips for Interviews. Tip one: If you didn't hear the question, don't panic. Say, Could you say that again, please? Examiners are happy to repeat. Tip two: If the question is difficult, you can take a little thinking time. Say, Let me see, or That's a good question. Then take a breath. Tip three: If you're not sure, say, I'm not sure, but I think, and then give your best idea. Tip four: Try not to stay silent for a long time. A short answer with a reason is better than no answer. Tip five: Speak clearly and look at the examiner. Don't mumble, and please don't eat pancakes!" What can you say if you didn't hear the question? Could you say that again, please? What can you say when you need thinking time? Let me see, or That's a good question. Then Birimo swallows and asks again clearly. What's your favorite season, and why? Kiko says, Let me see. I like spring, because the flowers come back. Next, Birimo asks Haru a tricky question. If you could have any animal as a friend, which would you choose? Haru says, That's a good question. I'm not sure, but I think I'd choose a dolphin. Now, phonics. Telephone has tele, which means far, like telescope. Paragraph has graph, which means write or draw, like autograph. Geography has geo, which means earth, like geology. Next time, we'll put everything together in a full mock interview.

vocab.ja: 模擬面接（本番の れんしゅう）

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Could you say that again, please? We've practiced every part of the interview: the self-introduction, the picture, the opinion, and asking again. Today is the big day: a mock interview（本番の れんしゅう）. Celeste changes the little room of light. Now there's a door, a desk, a clock and a stack of cards, just like a real test room. I sit behind the desk with a calm smile. At the end, I will say the words that finish every interview. Thank you. That's the end of the test. Say it with me. Thank you. That's the end of the test. Well done! Kiko goes first, and her hands are shaking. I say softly, Being nervous is normal. Take a breath and smile. Kiko knocks, walks in, says good morning and sits up straight. Then I give her the first card. Let's read the mock interview card. "Mock Interview Card. Please read this passage aloud. Kite Day. Every spring, the town of Brightfield holds a Kite Day by the river. Families bring kites of every shape and color, like fish, dragons and even birds. Children who don't have a kite can make one at a free workshop. Making a kite takes about an hour, and helpers show you each step. Many people say the best part is the moment their kite flies for the first time. Questions. One: Where is Kite Day held? Two: Look at the picture. What are the people doing? Three: Do you think children should spend more time outside? Why? Remember, take a breath, smile and do your best." Where is Kite Day held? By the river. How long does it take to make a kite? About an hour. Kiko reads slowly and clearly. She describes the families flying kites in the picture, and she gives her opinion with two reasons. Then I smile and say the last words. Haru, Riko and Birimo cheer. Suddenly, the third point of the star begins to shine like warm gold. The Ray of Courage lights up! Celeste says, Being brave doesn't mean you aren't nervous. It means you keep going. Shine on! Now, phonics. Let's review. Inspect has spect, which means look. Erupt has rupt, which means break. Audience has aud, which means hear. Rewrite has re, which means again. Next time, we'll talk about our wishes for the years ahead.

aiTask.goalJa: AI の エマ先生が 面接官の 模擬面接だよ。あいさつ → 短い 文を 声に だして 読む → 文の 質問 → 絵の 説明 → 意見と りゆう 2 つ、の じゅんで すすむよ。きこえなかったら Could you say that again, please? と いおう。AI が「Why?」と きいたら りゆうを いおう。ほんとうの なまえや 学校の なまえは いわなくて いいよ（ニックネームで OK）。6 かい いじょう やりとり しよう

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Thank you. That's the end of the test. Everyone finished the mock interview, and the third point of the star is shining brightly. Today, Celeste takes us to the Pool of Starlight again. Before, the pool showed us the past. Now Celeste says, This pool can also hold your wishes for the future. Say a wish out loud, and a little light will rise. Riko kneels by the water. She thinks for a moment and says, I hope to visit many countries someday. Say it with me. I hope to visit many countries someday. Beautiful! A tiny blue light floats up from the pool and dances above Riko's head. We use I hope to when we'd really like to do something in the future. I give everyone a star-shaped card, and we write our wishes together. Let's read our hope list. "Our Hope List. Haru: I hope to swim with dolphins someday, because they are my favorite sea animals. I also hope to see a real coral reef. Riko: I hope to visit many countries someday. I want to learn about different cultures and read stories in many languages. Kiko: I hope to play the flute on a big stage with children from other continents. Music is a language everyone understands. Birimo: I hope to taste pancakes in every country in the world. I will need a very big plate. Ms. Emma: I hope to keep learning new things with all of you, every single day." What does Haru hope to see? A real coral reef. Why does Kiko want to play music with other children? Because music is a language everyone understands. As we read each hope aloud, more lights rise from the pool. Soon, the air around us is full of tiny lights, blue and pink and gold. Celeste smiles at Birimo's light, which is shaped like a pancake. Now, phonics. In a speech, we pause after an opening phrase and stress its last important word. Six years aGO, pause. Good morning, EVeryone, pause. When I was SIX, pause. Next time, we'll imagine what we'll be like when we're twenty.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I hope to visit many countries someday. The air above the Pool of Starlight was full of tiny lights, one for every hope. Today, Celeste asks us a new question. Close your eyes and imagine you're twenty. What do you see? Birimo jumps up, puts on a pair of round glasses and a fake mustache, and says, I'm playing twenty-year-old Birimo! Everyone laughs. Then Riko closes her eyes, smiles and says, By the time I'm twenty, I'd like to speak three languages. Say it with me. By the time I'm twenty, I'd like to speak three languages. Great! By the time I'm twenty means before I become twenty, or when I'm twenty. You don't need to use it yourself yet. Just listen for it and understand it. I help everyone make a future plan. Let's read it. "Our Future Plan. Riko: By the time I'm twenty, I'd like to speak three languages. I'll keep reading books in English, and I'll start a new language, too. Haru: When I'm twenty, I'd like to study sea animals at a university. I'll probably still go swimming every weekend, even in winter. Kiko: When I'm older, I'd like to teach music to young children. At first, I was shy, but now I love sharing songs. Birimo: When I'm twenty, I'd like to flip ten pancakes at once and share them with everyone on the star. Most of all, we'd like to stay friends, no matter how old we are." What would Haru like to study? Sea animals. What would we like most of all? To stay friends. Kiko says, I'm a little worried. Twenty feels so far away. I nod. It's OK not to know everything now. Dreams can grow and change, just like you. Celeste rings softly, and the starlight in the pool shows four grown-up friends, laughing together. Birimo takes off his mustache and says, I like being me now, too. Now, phonics. In a speech, we pause after a linking phrase and stress its last word. At FIRST, pause. After a WHILE, pause. Most of ALL, pause. These little pauses help the audience follow your ideas. Next time, we'll talk about how we want to use English in our future.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, By the time I'm twenty, I'd like to speak three languages. We imagined our future selves, and Birimo looked very funny with his mustache. Today, Celeste waves her tiny arms, and the starlight forms moving pictures in the air. We see a scientist sharing a discovery with people from many countries. We see a doctor helping a traveler who is lost and worried. We see a pilot talking to the control tower, and a translator turning a story from one language into another. Celeste says, All of them use English in their careers. But English isn't only for work. It's also for friendship. Kiko watches a picture of children playing music together, and she says, I want to use English to make friends all over the world. Say it with me. I want to use English to make friends all over the world. Wonderful! After I want to use English to, we say what we want to do. Celeste shows us a glowing card. Let's read it. "Ways to Use English. You can use English to make friends all over the world. You can write to a pen pal on another continent, or chat with a new friend at a festival. You can use English to help people. Doctors, nurses and guides use it to help travelers. You can use English to learn. Many science books, websites and videos are in English. You can use English to share. Writers, musicians and scientists share their work with the world. Most of all, you can use English to understand people who are different from you. In the future, no matter what job you choose, English can open doors." Who uses English to help travelers? Doctors, nurses and guides. What can English do in the future, no matter what job you choose? It can open doors. Haru says he wants to use English to share his discoveries about the ocean. Riko wants to use English to read books from other countries, and maybe become a translator. Birimo says, I want to use English to order pancakes everywhere! I laugh. That's a real skill, too. Now, phonics. Thanks to YOU, pause. In the FUture, pause. No matter WHAT, pause. Stress the last important word, then take a short breath. Next time, we'll write letters to ourselves in ten years.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I want to use English to make friends all over the world. We talked about pen pals, translators, scientists and even ordering pancakes. Today, Celeste gives each of us a soft, glowing envelope. She says, Write a letter to yourself in ten years. I'll keep your letters inside the star like a time capsule. In ten years, your letter will find its way back to you. Riko looks at her empty paper and smiles. She writes the first line. Dear me in ten years, I hope you still love learning. Say it with me. Dear me in ten years, I hope you still love learning. Wonderful! A letter to your future self can ask questions, remember the past and give some kind advice. Haru lets us read his letter. Let's read it together. "Dear me in ten years, I hope you still love learning. Right now, I'm on the Star of Beginnings with Riko, Kiko, Birimo and Ms. Emma. Looking back, I've come such a long way. Six years ago, I could only say hello. Now, I can give presentations and answer questions in English. Are you studying the ocean now? Have you seen a real coral reef? Do you still swim every weekend? Remember how hard past tense verbs were for me? Went, ate, saw! I made lots of mistakes, but I kept going. So if something is difficult for you now, keep going, too. Before I finish, please say hello to Riko, Kiko and Birimo for me. I hope we're still friends, and I hope we're still laughing together. Shine on! Love, me." What was hard for Haru? Past tense verbs. What does Haru want his future self to say to his friends? Hello. Kiko writes about her flute, and Birimo writes a very short letter: Dear me, are there still pancakes? Love, Birimo. We seal our envelopes, and Celeste carries them gently into the heart of the star. Now, phonics. Before I FINish, pause. Looking BACK, pause. ToGETHer, pause. Say the strong part clearly, then take a short breath before you go on. Next time, the Future Dreams Fair opens on the star!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Dear me in ten years, I hope you still love learning. Celeste is keeping our letters safe inside the star. Today is the Future Dreams Fair! The silver grass is full of booths made of light, and hundreds of tiny lights from the star float around like curious visitors. Each of us has a booth with a sign. Haru's booth is first. He has drawn a deep blue sea with glowing fish, and he says proudly, In the future, I'd like to study the ocean because I love sea animals. Say it with me. In the future, I'd like to study the ocean because I love sea animals. Fantastic! Let's read the booth signs. "Future Dreams Fair. Booth 1, Haru: In the future, I'd like to study the ocean because I love sea animals. Ever since Deep Sea City, I've wanted to explore places where light never reaches. Booth 2, Riko: I'd like to write children's books and translate stories, so children everywhere can enjoy them. Booth 3, Kiko: I'd like to be a music teacher and play the flute with children around the world. Booth 4, Birimo: I'd like to be a pancake chef on a spaceship. Pancakes taste better with a view of the stars! A note from Ms. Emma: Dreams can change, and that's OK. Keep learning, and your dream will grow with you." Why does Haru want to study the ocean? Because he loves sea animals. What does Ms. Emma say about dreams? Dreams can change, and that's OK. When we read Birimo's sign, everyone bursts out laughing, and Birimo takes a bow. Then Kiko asks me, What if I want a different dream next year? I smile. Then you'll have a new adventure. Six years ago, you didn't know you'd stand here. Suddenly, the fourth point of the star begins to glow, soft and pink like a sunrise. The Ray of Dreams lights up! Celeste says, Your dreams make the star brighter. Shine on! Now, phonics. Let's review. Six years aGO, pause. Most of ALL, pause. Looking BACK, pause. Predict has dict, which means say. Next time, we'll say thank you to the friends who helped us along the way.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, In the future, I'd like to study the ocean because I love sea animals. After the Future Dreams Fair, four rays of the star are shining: Memories, Growth, Courage and Dreams. Two rays are still dim. Celeste rings softly like a tiny bell. Before the next ray shines, she says, think of everyone who helped you. Kiko looks at Haru, Riko and Birimo. She remembers the day she was too nervous to speak, and Riko held her hand. Haru remembers the long words he couldn't read, and Kiko read them with him slowly. Riko remembers getting lost in the Labyrinth of Tales, and Birimo kept everyone laughing. Kiko says, I couldn't have done it without you. Say it with me. I couldn't have done it without you. Wonderful! Celeste gives each of us a glass jar of light. Whisper a thank-you into it, she says, and the light will fly to anyone. Haru writes to our old guides. Let's read them. "Dear Ember, thank you for teaching us to be brave on the Island of Fire. Dear Skye, thank you for showing us the sky and helping us talk with travelers. Dear Olive, thank you for teaching us to share our opinions and listen kindly. Dear Lumi and Dr. Vale, thank you for our first research presentation under the sea. Dear Nib, thank you for reminding us that everyone has a story to tell. Dear Puff and Grandma Rowan, thank you for teaching us to name our feelings, and for the warmest pancakes ever. Dear Orbit, thank you for showing us that every voice counts. We will never forget you. With love and gratitude, Haru, Riko, Kiko and Birimo." Who taught us to name our feelings? Puff and Grandma Rowan. What did Orbit show us? That every voice counts. We whisper into the jars and open the lids. Whoosh! Tiny lights fly away like shooting stars. Far away, a tiny blue light blinks back. Maybe it's Lumi! Now, phonics. Right starts with R, so your tongue doesn't touch anything. Light starts with L, so your tongue touches behind your top teeth. Read starts with R, too, but lead, as in lead the way, starts with L. Very starts with V. Put your top teeth on your lower lip. Berry starts with B, with your lips together. Next time, we'll plan a secret surprise for someone very special.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I couldn't have done it without you. This morning, Riko has an idea. She whispers, We thanked our friends and our guides, but who has been with us every single day for six years? Ms. Emma! Let's make a surprise for her. Birimo's job is to keep me busy. He holds up a spoon like a microphone and asks, Ms. Emma, how do you make the fluffiest pancakes in the world? Do you flip them once or twice? What about blueberries? I laugh and start to explain. Behind a silver bush, Haru, Riko and Kiko make a card with ribbons and stickers. Kiko writes the most important line. Thank you for always believing in us. Say it with me. Thank you for always believing in us. Beautiful! When Birimo runs out of questions, everyone jumps out and shouts, Surprise! Let's read the card. "Dear Ms. Emma, six years ago, we met you in the Forest of Beginnings. We could only say hello, but you smiled as if we were already great speakers. You taught us four magic words, and then thousands more. When we made mistakes, you said, Mistakes help us grow. When we were nervous, you stood right next to us. You read stories with us, sang songs with us, and laughed at all of Birimo's jokes, even the very silly ones. Thanks to you, we can read books, tell stories and share our ideas in English. Thank you for always believing in us. You are the best teacher in every world. With love, Haru, Riko, Kiko and Birimo. P.S. Birimo really wants your pancake recipe." Where did we first meet Ms. Emma? In the Forest of Beginnings. What did Ms. Emma say when we made mistakes? Mistakes help us grow. I read the card twice. My eyes get shiny, and a happy tear rolls down my cheek. I hug all four of them. I say, These are happy tears. I'm so proud of you. Now, phonics. Vest starts with V, so put your top teeth on your lower lip. Best starts with B, with your lips together. Think starts with TH. Put your tongue between your teeth and blow. Sink starts with S, with your tongue behind your teeth. Three is TH plus R. Free starts with F, and tree starts with T. Next time, we'll start writing a very important speech.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Thank you for always believing in us. Today, Celeste has big news. In one week, we will have our graduation here on the Star of Beginnings, and one student will give the graduation speech. Who should it be? Haru says, I vote for Kiko! She used to be so nervous, but now she speaks so clearly. Riko and Birimo raise their hands, too. Kiko's eyes go wide. Me? She is a little scared, but she says yes, as long as everyone helps her. We sit in a circle and make an outline: the past, the journey, thank-yous and the future. Kiko thinks for a while. Then she writes the very first line. Six years ago, I didn't know any English. Say it with me. Six years ago, I didn't know any English. Wonderful! Then everyone adds one line. Let's read the first draft. "Six years ago, I didn't know any English. I was shy, and I was afraid of making mistakes. Then, in the Forest of Beginnings, I met my friends and my teacher, and our journey began. At first, we could only say hello. After a while, we could ask questions, read books and tell stories. We visited many worlds and met many wonderful guides. Haru taught us that mistakes help us learn. Riko taught us that every person has a story worth sharing. Birimo taught us that laughing together makes hard things easier. Most of all, Ms. Emma taught us to believe in ourselves. Looking back, I am proud of how much we have grown. Graduation is not the last page of our story. Together, we will keep reading, keep singing and keep talking in English. Thank you, everyone." Who taught us that every person has a story worth sharing? Riko. What did Ms. Emma teach us? To believe in ourselves. Birimo asks, Can I add a line about pancakes? Everyone laughs. Maybe in the next draft, Birimo! Now, phonics. She starts with SH, so round your lips and push the air out. See starts with S, with a smile. Fall starts with F. Put your top teeth on your lower lip. Hall starts with H, which is just air. Hat has a wide sound, so open your mouth wide. Hut has a short, relaxed sound. Next time, Kiko will practice her speech in front of all of us.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Six years ago, I didn't know any English. Today is rehearsal day. Celeste waves her tiny arms, and the silver grass rises into a small round stage with a soft spotlight of starlight. Kiko walks up with her speech in her hands. The rest of us sit in front of the stage. Birimo sits in the back row and shouts, I'm playing the audience! All of it! Kiko begins. Six years ago, I didn't know any English. But she reads very fast and looks only at her paper. When she finishes, she sighs. Oh no, I went way too fast. I smile and point to three places in the speech. Pause here. Smile. Look at the audience. Say it with me. Pause here. Smile. Look at the audience. Excellent! Then I give Kiko a little card. Let's read the rehearsal tips. "Rehearsal Tips. One: Stand up straight. Good posture helps your voice sound strong. Two: Speak slowly. When we are nervous, we often speak too fast, so slow down a little more than you think. Three: Pause here. After an important line, stop for a moment and let your words reach everyone. Four: Smile. A smile helps you relax, and it helps the audience relax, too. Five: Look at the audience. Make eye contact with a few friendly faces, near and far. Six: It's OK to be nervous. Even great speakers feel butterflies in their stomachs. Take a deep breath and remember why your words matter. Last tip: Practice, practice, practice, and then enjoy it!" Why should you smile? It helps you and the audience relax. What can you do when you feel nervous? Take a deep breath. Kiko tries again. This time, she speaks slowly, pauses after six years ago, and looks right at Birimo in the back row. When she finishes, we all clap and cheer. Birimo says, I heard every word! I got goosebumps! Kiko laughs. She is still nervous, but now she is excited, too. Now, phonics. World has the ER sound and then an L. Word has no L. Walk has an aw sound, and the L is silent. Work has the ER sound. Heard has ER, too, but hard has AR, so open your mouth wide. Next time, Celeste will tell us a story that will surprise everyone, especially Birimo.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Pause here. Smile. Look at the audience. Tonight, we all sit around the Pool of Starlight. Five rays of the star are shining above us. Celeste looks at Birimo with the same gentle smile she has given him since the first day. Then she rings softly and says, It's time for a story. A true story. Let's read Celeste's story. "Six years ago, a tiny light lived here on the Star of Beginnings. One morning, it looked down through the clouds and saw a quiet green forest. Children were starting their journey with words there, and some of them looked a little shy. The tiny light wanted to help them. So it floated down, down, down, all the way to the Forest of Beginnings, and it became a small, playful creature who loved to laugh. It carried a piece of starlight in its heart. That is why its map glowed, and why the map always knew the way. It stayed close to the children, cheered them on, and made them laugh on hard days. Do you know who that tiny light was? It was Birimo." Everyone turns to Birimo. His cheeks turn pink. Haru whispers, So Birimo had been watching over us all along. Say it with me. Birimo had been watching over us all along. Wonderful! Why did the tiny light float down? To help the children starting their journey. Why did the map always know the way? Because Birimo carried a piece of starlight in his heart. Birimo smiles shyly. I forgot! I was having so much fun with you that I forgot where I came from. I just loved being your friend. Celeste says, You may come home to the star now, little light. Everyone is quiet. Birimo looks at us and shakes his head. My home is wherever my friends are! Celeste laughs like a little bell and says, Then stay with them. Shine on! Suddenly, the fifth ray begins to glow, warm and golden. The Ray of Thanks lights up! Now, phonics. Let's review. Very starts with V, with your top teeth on your lower lip. Think starts with TH, with your tongue between your teeth. World has ER and then L. Thanks to you: stress YOU, then pause. Thanks to you, I had the best six years. Next time, we can talk about anything we like!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Birimo had been watching over us all along. This morning, Birimo is still Birimo. He wakes up first, does a happy dance on the silver grass and asks if stars have pancakes for breakfast. We all laugh. Some things will never change, and we're glad. I bring out a big colorful wheel. I say, Today is free-talk day. There are no tests and no scripts. Just friends talking. Let's talk about anything you like! Say it with me. Let's talk about anything you like! Great! I point to the card under the wheel. Let's read it. "The Free-Talk Topic Wheel. Spin the wheel and talk about the topic it lands on: hobbies, food, books, dreams, funny memories or your favorite worlds. Here are three tips for great free talk. First, answer with more than one sentence. Don't just say, Yes, I do. Add a reason or an example. Second, ask a follow-up question, like, Why do you like it? or, What happened next? Third, react to your friend. Say things like, No way!, That's awesome!, or, Same here! A conversation is like playing catch. You throw a question, your friend catches it and throws something back. If you drop the ball, just pick it up and smile. There are no wrong topics today. Enjoy it!" What should you add after a short answer? A reason or an example. What is a conversation like? Playing catch. Birimo spins first, and of course, the wheel lands on food. Haru gets funny memories, and he tells the story of the day Birimo tried to fly a kite in the rain. Riko gets books, and Kiko asks her three follow-up questions in a row. Celeste listens from the top of the wheel and rings happily every time someone says, No way! At first, free talk felt hard, but now our words come out easily, like water from a spring. Now, phonics. Let's review. Play ends with a, y. Dislike is dis plus like, and dis means the opposite. Construct has struct, which means build. At first: stress FIRST, then pause. At first, I was shy. Read starts with R, so your tongue doesn't touch anything. Next time, we'll tell the story of our six-year journey.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let's talk about anything you like! Today, Celeste has a special request. Every journey that begins here becomes a story, she says, and this star keeps those stories. Will you tell me yours? Riko jumps up. She loves telling stories more than anything. She thinks for a moment, smiles, and begins with the most famous words in storytelling. Once upon a time, four friends found a map. Say it with me. Once upon a time, four friends found a map. Fantastic! Haru adds the middle, Kiko adds the feelings, and Birimo adds the sound effects. Then I write it all down. Let's read our story. "Once upon a time, four friends found a map. Well, actually, they met long before that, in the Forest of Beginnings, when they could only say hello. One day, in the Kingdom of English, Birimo found an old map of worlds that were not on any map yet. The map began to glow, and with their teacher, the friends followed it from world to world. They crossed bridges, climbed mountains, rode trains above the clouds and traveled deep under the sea. They solved riddles, performed plays, invented machines and wrote their own stories. Sometimes the journey was hard, and they made lots of mistakes. But they helped each other with kindness, and they kept going. At last, a beam of light carried them up to a star, where every journey begins. And the story? It isn't finished yet." Where did Birimo find the map? In the Kingdom of English. What did the friends do when the journey was hard? They helped each other and kept going. Celeste listens with her eyes closed. When the story ends, she lowers the pages gently into the Pool of Starlight. The words turn into tiny lights and form a new chapter in the water. I say, A good story has a beginning, a middle and an ending, but the best stories leave room for more. Now, phonics. Let's review. Green has double e. Kindness is kind plus n, e, s, s, which makes a noun. Transport has port, which means carry. When I was six: stress SIX, then pause. When I was six, I met my best friends. She starts with SH, so round your lips. Next time, we'll give opinion speeches about learning languages.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Once upon a time, four friends found a map. Today, Celeste asks us a big question. Why do people learn languages? I say this is a perfect question for an opinion speech. A good opinion speech has four parts. First, say your opinion. Next, give your reasons. Then, give an example. Finally, say your opinion again. We each write a short speech. Riko goes first. She stands tall, smiles at the audience and says, I believe that learning languages connects people. Say it with me. I believe that learning languages connects people. Excellent! Let's read Riko's speech. "I believe that learning languages connects people. I have two reasons. First, when you speak someone's language, even a little, they smile and open their hearts. Second, learning a language helps you understand how other people think and feel. Here is an example. At the World Round Table, I met Priya, who lives far away. At first, we were both shy, and it seemed impossible to become friends. But we tried English together. She taught me a song from her home, and I taught her a game from mine. Soon we were laughing like old friends. Language made the invisible wall between us disappear. No matter what language you learn, it can build a bridge to someone new. That's why I believe that learning languages connects people." How many reasons does Riko give? Two. What made the invisible wall disappear? Language. Then Haru speaks. He believes that languages help us learn about the world, because there are amazing books and ideas in every language. Kiko believes that music and words together can reach any heart. Birimo stands up proudly. I believe that pancakes connect people! Everyone laughs, but then he gives a good reason. When you share food, you share stories, too. I nod. That's actually a good point. Now, phonics. Let's review. Shirt has i, r, which sounds the same as e, r and u, r. Impossible is i, m plus possible, and i, m means not before a p. Visible has vis, which means see. No matter what: stress WHAT, then pause. No matter what happens, keep learning. Walk has a silent L. Next time, it will be the night before our graduation.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I believe that learning languages connects people. Tonight is graduation eve. Celeste dims the floating lights, and the sky above the star fills with more stars than we can count. We lie down on the soft silver grass with warm blankets, side by side, and look up. Nobody talks for a while. Then Haru says, I can't believe this is our last night before graduation. Kiko says she feels a little sad, because something special is ending. Riko says she feels excited, too. Birimo yawns a huge yawn and says, I'm sleepy... Everyone laughs, because that is exactly what he said in our very first week. I sit up and smile at everyone. I say, It's OK to feel sad and excited at the same time. Tomorrow, a new journey begins. Say it with me. Tomorrow, a new journey begins. Beautiful! Then I give everyone a small card. Let's read the goodnight page. "A Goodnight Page. Tonight, close your eyes and remember. Remember the first time you said hello, and the first book you read all the way to the end. Remember the riddles, the songs, the plays and the stories you wrote. Remember the days when English felt hard, and how you kept going anyway. It's OK to feel a little sad tonight. Something special is ending. It's also OK to feel excited, because something new is starting. Tomorrow, you will graduate, but learning never really stops. There will always be new books to read, new songs to sing and new friends to talk with. So sleep well, my brave learners. Tomorrow, a new journey begins. With love, Ms. Emma." Why is it OK to feel excited? Because something new is starting. What will there always be? New books, new songs and new friends. Just then, a shooting star flies across the sky, and we all make a wish. Now, phonics. Let's review. Knee has a silent k. Preview is pre plus view, and pre means before. Telephone has tele, which means far. In the future: stress the start of future, then pause. In the future, I'll keep reading. Fall starts with F, so put your top teeth on your lower lip. Hall is just air. Next time is our graduation day, the very last lesson of our six years!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Tomorrow, a new journey begins. Today is the day! This is our 1,200th lesson, and it's graduation day on the Star of Beginnings. The silver grass sparkles, and the Pool of Starlight shows our families far below, watching and waving. Then little lights fly up from every world. Orbit, Puff, Nib, Lumi, Olive, Skye and Ember have all come to say congratulations! Celeste rings her bell, and Kiko walks to the front. She pauses, smiles and looks at the audience. Let's read her speech. "Six years ago, I didn't know any English. Today, I am standing here with my best friends. When I was little, I was too shy to speak. Now, I can share my ideas with the whole world. We made lots of mistakes, but we never gave up, and we were never alone. Thank you, Haru, for making us brave. Thank you, Riko, for your wonderful stories. Thank you, Birimo, for watching over us and making us laugh. Thank you, Ms. Emma, for always believing in us. And thank you to every guide in every world. Today, we graduate, but our learning doesn't stop. This is not the end. It's a new beginning!" Who did Kiko thank for making us laugh? Birimo. Does our learning stop today? No, it doesn't! Everyone cheers. I give everyone a graduation certificate and a tiny star pin. Birimo says his pin looks a little like a pancake. Then I say, One last time, our four magic words! Look! Stop! Come here! Go! Suddenly, the sixth ray begins to shine. The Ray of Beginnings lights up! All six rays are shining, and the star shines brighter than ever before. Celeste gives us a brand-new map, but it is completely blank. The places will appear as you keep learning, she says. Haru smiles. This is not the end. It's a new beginning! Say it with me. This is not the end. It's a new beginning! Now, phonics. Let's review six years of sounds. Light has igh, and your tongue touches behind your top teeth. Comfortable is comfort plus able. Paragraph has graph, which means write. Together: stress GETH, then pause. Together, we grew. Right starts with R, so your tongue doesn't touch anything. I say, Keep reading stories, singing songs and talking every day. Celeste rings one last time. Shine on!

lines.speaker: Ms. Emma
lines.en: Congratulations, graduates! Here are your certificates and your tiny star pins.
lines.ja: 卒業 おめでとう！ 卒業証書と 小さな 星の ピンよ。

lines.speaker: Haru
lines.en: Thank you so much, Ms. Emma! Wow, look! Lights are coming from every world. Is that Orbit?
lines.ja: ほんとうに ありがとう、エマ先生！ わあ、見て！ どの ワールドからも 光が きてる。あれ、オービット？

lines.speaker: Riko
lines.en: Yes! And Puff, Nib and Lumi, too. They all came to see us graduate.
lines.ja: そう！ パフも ニブも ルミも。みんな 卒業を 見に きて くれたんだ。

lines.speaker: Birimo
lines.en: My star pin is the shiniest. It looks a little like a pancake!
lines.ja: ぼくの 星の ピンが いちばん ピカピカ。ちょっと パンケーキみたい！

lines.speaker: Kiko
lines.en: Ha ha! Everyone, let's say the four magic words one last time. Look! Stop! Come here! Go!
lines.ja: あはは！ みんな、4 つの まほうの ことばを さいごに もう いちど。見て！ とまって！ こっちに きて！ いって！

lines.speaker: Ms. Emma
lines.en: Look! The sixth ray! The Ray of Beginnings lit up! All six rays are shining!
lines.ja: 見て！ 6 つめの 光の 先！ はじまりの 光が ともったわ！ 6 つ ぜんぶ かがやいてる！

lines.speaker: Riko
lines.en: Celeste is giving us a new map, but it's completely blank. Why?
lines.ja: セレストが あたらしい 地図を くれるけど、まっしろ。どうして？

lines.speaker: Haru
lines.en: Because the places will appear as we keep learning. This is not the end. It's a new beginning!
lines.ja: まなびつづけると、場所が あらわれるからだよ。これで おわりじゃない。あたらしい はじまりだ！

lines.speaker: Birimo
lines.en: Then where should we go first? I vote for somewhere with pancakes!
lines.ja: じゃあ さいしょは どこへ いく？ ぼくは パンケーキの ある ところに 一票！

lines.speaker: Kiko
lines.en: Wherever we go, we'll go together. Shine on!
lines.ja: どこへ いっても、いっしょに いこう。Shine on!

aiTask.goalJa: AI の セレストと グランドフィナーレ！ 6 年間で いちばんの 思い出と、これから 英語で やりたい ことを 話そう。セレストが「Why?」「What will you do next?」と きいたら りゆうや これからの ことを いおう。さいごに This is not the end. It's a new beginning! と いおう。6 かい いじょう やりとり しよう
aiTask.starterEn: Let's pretend I'm Celeste. Congratulations, graduate! Shine on! All six rays are shining, and here is your new blank map. Looking back on your six years, what's your favorite memory?
